Moses, the man God sent to bring Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), is a big name, so I get why he came to mind. But Paul doesn't name him here. He says the Gentiles were separate from Christ. Keep your eyes on that one name, baker.

Abraham, the man God promised a great nation (Genesis 12:2), is a big name in this neighborhood, so that pick makes sense. But Paul doesn't say it here. He says they were separate from Christ. That's the one he puts on the list.
Paul says the opposite. He says that at that time they were "…without hope and without God in the world." That's a hard line. The good news is coming right behind it, so hang in there with me.

Paul says it the other way around. "But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far away have been brought near through the blood of Christ." Far away is where they were, and near is where they are now. That little word "now" changes everything.

explanations.answer: those far away and those near
explanations.explanation: That's right. Paul says Christ preached "…peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near." He didn't pick a side of the room. Peace went to both.
Paul says it wider than that. Christ preached "…peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near." Those near got it, and so did those far away. Nobody was left out of that sentence.

explanations.answer: only those who were far away
explanations.explanation: The far away are in there, and Paul spends plenty of time on them. But he says Christ preached "…peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near." Both groups are named. Peace was for the near ones too.

Paul says it plainly. "For through Him we both have access to the Father by one Spirit." Both groups get access, and it all comes through Christ. I'd call that good news, baker.

Travelers is a good-sounding word, but it isn't Paul's. He says they are "…no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints…" The word he lands on is citizens. So travelers doesn't fit the blank, baker.
